title: Fluid, electrolyte and acid-base balance
blurb: Place body water in its compartments, match Na⁺, K⁺ and Ca²⁺ to their jobs, predict what ADH, aldosterone, RAAS and ANP do, and explain how buffers, lungs and kidneys hold blood pH at 7.35–7.45.
question: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has a blood pH of 7.28 and is breathing fast and deep. Is this acidosis or alkalosis, why has her breathing changed, and which defense will take longest to correct her pH?

teach.body: Formally, fluid balance means intake matches output and water is shared correctly between the intracellular fluid (ICF, inside cells, the larger share) and the extracellular fluid (ECF: plasma plus interstitial fluid). Water crosses between them by osmosis, toward the side with more solute. In plain English: water follows salt. The kidneys decide how much water and salt the body keeps, and with the lungs they hold blood pH in a narrow range.

teach.caption: Water moves between compartments by osmosis, toward the higher solute concentration.

teach.body: Maria, who has type 1 diabetes, arrives with ketoacidosis and a blood pH of 7.28: below 7.35, so acidosis, and metabolic because ketone acids are the cause. Her bicarbonate buffer soaks up H⁺ within seconds. Within minutes her lungs compensate: deep, fast breathing blows off CO₂ and raises pH. Over hours to days her kidneys do the heavy lifting, secreting H⁺ into the urine and reabsorbing bicarbonate.

teach.text: Sodium is the main EXTRAcellular cation; potassium is the main INTRAcellular one. HYPERventilation causes ALKALOSIS. Buffers act FASTEST; kidneys act SLOWEST. ADH DECREASES urine volume. Aldosterone keeps Na⁺ and SECRETES K⁺. Renin is a kidney ENZYME, not an adrenal hormone. Blood at pH 7.0 is acidotic, not neutral and healthy.

items: Most body water is intracellular; ECF = plasma + interstitial fluid; water follows salt.
Na⁺ outside cells (ECF volume), K⁺ inside (excitability), Ca²⁺ for bone, clotting and contraction.
ADH: keep water. Aldosterone: keep Na⁺, lose K⁺. ANP: lose Na⁺ and water. PTH: keep Ca²⁺.
RAAS: renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II; blood pressure rises.
Blood pH 7.35–7.45; buffers (seconds), lungs (minutes, CO₂), kidneys (days, H⁺ and HCO₃⁻).

summary: You can now place body water in its compartments, match sodium, potassium and calcium to their roles, and predict how ADH, aldosterone, ANP and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system change urine and blood pressure. You can also classify acidosis and alkalosis and rank the buffer, lung and kidney defenses of blood pH.

A.q: Which body fluid compartment holds most of the body's water?
A.why: Most body water lies inside cells, in the intracellular fluid. The extracellular fluid (plasma plus interstitial fluid) holds the smaller share.

whyNot.0: Interstitial fluid is part of the extracellular fluid, which is the smaller share of body water.
whyNot.2: Plasma is only part of the extracellular fluid, a small fraction of total body water.
whyNot.3: Lymph is interstitial fluid returning to the blood; its volume at any moment is small.

A.q: Which electrolyte is the main cation of the extracellular fluid and largely sets its volume?
A.why: Sodium is the main extracellular cation. Because water follows sodium, the amount of sodium in the ECF largely determines its volume.

whyNot.0: Potassium is the main intracellular cation, not the extracellular one.
whyNot.1: Calcium is stored mostly in bone; it is not the main ECF cation.
whyNot.3: Chloride is the main extracellular anion (negative), not a cation.

A.q: An arterial blood sample has a pH of 7.30. How should it be classified?
A.why: Normal blood pH is 7.35–7.45. A value below 7.35 is acidosis, even though 7.30 is above the neutral value of 7.

whyNot.0: Normal blood is slightly basic, but its range is 7.35–7.45, and 7.30 falls below it.
whyNot.1: Alkalosis is a pH above 7.45; 7.30 is below the normal range.
whyNot.3: Healthy blood is never slightly acidic; 7.30 is below 7.35, which is acidosis.

B.q: A hiker has not drunk water for hours, and her blood solute concentration rises. Which hormone increases, and where does it act?
B.why: Concentrated blood triggers ADH release from the posterior pituitary. ADH inserts aquaporins in the collecting ducts, so more water returns to the blood and urine becomes scant and concentrated.

whyNot.1: Aldosterone responds mainly to low blood pressure and high K⁺, and it reabsorbs sodium rather than water directly.
whyNot.2: ADH is the right hormone, but it acts on the collecting duct; the proximal tubule reabsorbs water without it.
whyNot.3: ANP makes the kidneys lose sodium and water, which would worsen dehydration.

B.q: Aldosterone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct. What is its effect?
B.why: Aldosterone makes the DCT and collecting duct reabsorb sodium (water follows) and secrete potassium.

whyNot.0: The ions are reversed: aldosterone keeps sodium and gets rid of potassium.
whyNot.1: Inserting aquaporins in the collecting duct is the action of ADH.
whyNot.2: Calcium reabsorption is driven by PTH, not aldosterone.

B.q: During an anxiety attack, a patient breathes rapidly for several minutes. Which acid-base change results?
B.why: Hyperventilation blows off CO₂. Less CO₂ means less carbonic acid, so pH rises: respiratory alkalosis, because the cause is breathing.

whyNot.0: Respiratory acidosis comes from hypoventilation, when CO₂ builds up.
whyNot.1: The cause here is breathing, which changes CO₂, so the disturbance is respiratory, not metabolic.
whyNot.3: Losing CO₂ raises pH, and the cause is respiratory, so this is neither acidosis nor metabolic.

C.q: Which sequence correctly shows the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system after blood pressure falls?
options: Renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II, aldosterone
ACE, angiotensin I, renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone
Renin, angiotensin II, ACE, angiotensin I, aldosterone
Aldosterone, renin, angiotensin I, ACE, angiotensin II
C.why: Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; ACE converts that to angiotensin II, which triggers aldosterone release.

whyNot.1: Renin acts first; ACE acts on angiotensin I, which renin has to produce.
whyNot.2: Angiotensin I comes before angiotensin II; ACE converts I into II.
whyNot.3: Aldosterone is released at the end, in response to angiotensin II.

C.q: In diabetic ketoacidosis, ketone acids lower blood pH. Which pair of compensations is expected?
options: Faster, deeper breathing; kidneys secrete more H⁺
Slower breathing; kidneys secrete more H⁺
Faster, deeper breathing; kidneys lose bicarbonate
Slower breathing; kidneys lose more bicarbonate
C.why: Ketoacidosis is a metabolic acidosis. The lungs compensate within minutes by breathing faster and deeper to blow off CO₂; the kidneys compensate over hours to days by secreting H⁺ and reabsorbing bicarbonate.

whyNot.1: Slower breathing would keep CO₂ in the blood and lower the pH further.
whyNot.2: The breathing change is right, but losing bicarbonate would remove buffer base and deepen the acidosis.
whyNot.3: Both parts are wrong: slower breathing retains CO₂, and losing bicarbonate worsens acidosis.

C.q: Days of repeated vomiting remove large amounts of hydrochloric acid from the stomach. Which disturbance is most likely?
C.why: Losing stomach acid removes H⁺ from the body, so bicarbonate is left relatively high and pH rises. The cause is not breathing, so it is metabolic alkalosis.

whyNot.0: Losing acid raises pH rather than lowering it, so this is not acidosis.
whyNot.1: The pH does rise, but the cause is acid loss from the gut, not a change in breathing.
whyNot.2: Respiratory acidosis comes from CO₂ retention by poor ventilation, not from vomiting.

reteach.title: Keeping a fish tank healthy
reteach.question: Picture keeping a home aquarium steady: topping up water, dosing salt, adding pH buffer, running the air pump and doing water changes. How does each job match the body's fluid and pH controls?

blocks.body: Topping up evaporated water is thirst and ADH. Dosing salt is aldosterone keeping sodium, and water follows the salt. Buffer powder stops the pH from jumping the moment something acidic drops in, just like bicarbonate in blood. The air pump vents gas within minutes, as the lungs vent CO₂. A partial water change is slow but resets everything, like the kidneys secreting H⁺ and keeping bicarbonate.

blocks.text: The fastest fix is not the strongest: buffers act first, but only the kidneys can remove excess acid from the body for good.

explain.body: Most body water is intracellular. The extracellular fluid is plasma plus interstitial fluid. Water moves by osmosis toward more solute, so water follows salt. Sodium is the main ECF cation and sets ECF volume; potassium is the main ICF cation and governs nerve and heart excitability; calcium serves bone, clotting and muscle contraction.

test.q: Which statement about body fluids is correct?
options: Most of the body's water is in the plasma
Sodium is the main cation inside cells
Plasma and interstitial fluid form the ECF
Water moves toward the lower solute level
test.why: The extracellular fluid is plasma plus interstitial fluid. Most water is intracellular, potassium is the main intracellular cation, and water moves toward the higher solute concentration.

whyNot.0: Most body water is inside cells; plasma is a small part of the extracellular fluid.
whyNot.1: Potassium is the main intracellular cation; sodium dominates outside cells.
whyNot.3: By osmosis, water moves toward the higher solute concentration.

explain.body: ADH from the posterior pituitary adds aquaporins in the collecting duct: less, more concentrated urine. Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex keeps Na⁺ and secretes K⁺. ANP from stretched heart atria makes the kidneys shed Na⁺ and water. PTH increases Ca²⁺ reabsorption.

test.q: Which hormone makes the kidneys excrete more sodium and water, lowering blood pressure?
test.why: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), from the heart's atria, increases sodium and water loss, so blood volume and pressure fall.

whyNot.0: ADH increases water reabsorption, which raises blood volume.
whyNot.1: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption, with water following.
whyNot.3: Renin starts RAAS, which raises blood pressure.

explain.body: When blood pressure or sodium falls, juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney release the enzyme renin. Renin turns angiotensinogen (from the liver) into angiotensin I; ACE, mostly in the lungs, makes angiotensin II. Angiotensin II constricts vessels and triggers aldosterone, ADH and thirst, so blood pressure rises.

test.q: Renin is released in response to low blood pressure by which cells?
options: Muscle cells of the heart atria
test.why: Renin is an enzyme released by the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney when blood pressure or sodium is low; it starts RAAS.

whyNot.0: The adrenal cortex releases aldosterone later in the pathway, not renin.
whyNot.2: Atrial cells release ANP, which lowers blood pressure.
whyNot.3: The posterior pituitary releases ADH, not renin.

explain.body: Normal blood pH is 7.35–7.45. Below is acidosis; above is alkalosis. Buffers (mainly bicarbonate) act in seconds; the lungs change CO₂ in minutes; the kidneys secrete H⁺ and keep or make bicarbonate over hours to days. Respiratory problems change CO₂; metabolic problems change bicarbonate or the acid load.

test.q: Which defense against a change in blood pH is the slowest but the most powerful?
test.why: The kidneys take hours to days, but they can remove H⁺ from the body and rebuild bicarbonate, so they are the most powerful defense.

whyNot.0: The bicarbonate buffer is the fastest defense, acting in seconds, but its capacity is limited.
whyNot.1: The lungs act within minutes by changing CO₂; they are faster than the kidneys.
whyNot.3: Plasma proteins act as buffers, working within seconds; they are not the slow, powerful defense.
